newsitem.title: CHINA: Prodigy says China internet service to start soon.
newsitem.headline: Prodigy says China internet service to start soon.

text.p: U.S. firm Prodigy Inc has hit some regulatory snags in its plans to provide Internet services through a joint venture in China, but subscribers should be on-line soon, company officials said on Friday.

Users who have signed up for the venture's Internet services should be surfing the worldwide computer network within 30 days, said Bruce Franson, Prodigy Innternational vice president for the Asia Pacific region.

Prodigy announced the joint venture on April 29, but "regulatory grey areas" had slowed the launch of its services, which will initially be limited to the Shanghai area, Franson said in a telephone interview.
"We're definitely going ahead and we're moving as fast as we can," he said, but declined to elaborate on the reasons for the delay.
"That 30 days is a target, but my expectation is that it's very realistic," he said from his U.S. office.
The new venture had rung alarm bells among Chinese regulators who were trying to ensure tight controls on Internet service providers, industry sources said.
China banned foreign companies, including joint ventures, from directly providing Internet services in China, an official with the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications (MPT) said.
But foreign firms could supply equipment, technology and expertise to a Chinese partner, who would in turn provide the Internet services to its subscribers, industry executives said.
Prodigy owned 80 percent of the joint venture with the other 20 percent held by the China North Industries Corp (Norinco) Group, Franson said.
The U.S. company planned to invest $50 million in the venture over the next three years, he said.
The joint venture, to be registered in Singapore, would use Prodigy's technology, software and content, said an official from the Chinese partner, Norinco's Shentong Telecommunication Co Ltd.

"We're (Prodigy) involved in the investment but we're not involved in the management," Franson said. "The operating company is using the technology and content of Prodigy but essentially operating the business on its own."
The venture had already pre-signed clients numbering in the thousands, who would pay 270 yuan ($32.53) for 30 hours of on-line time, he said.
Prodigy is pitting itself against the telecommunications ministry, whose subsidiary Chinanet is currently the country's main Internet provider.

As well as acting as service provider, the MPT was also responsible for making sure mainland users could not access sites deemed subversive, a Chinese official involved in setting Internet policy said on Friday.
Access is routinely blocked to overseas news sources, pornographic sites and discussion groups used by Chinese in the mainland and abroad as a way to exchange political views.

Chinese Internet surfers who tried to visit one politically oriented site on June 4, the anniversary of the army's 1989 crackdown on student-led protests in Beijing, could only reach a screen with the English word "Forbidden".
"Some addresses are being filtered, so you are not allowed to enter," the Chinese Internet official said. "They have too much news and (could) have an influence on things in China."
